label: Similarity in the Euclidean Plane
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 67 to 76 and places similarity between congruence and affine freedom. A similarity preserves all angles and scales every length by one positive factor, yet it may keep or reverse orientation. We classify these maps, find their fixed centers, and apply them to classical triangle geometry across the plane.

label: What a Similarity Preserves
notes: A similarity is weaker than an isometry but still rigid in shape: it multiplies every distance by the same ratio k and leaves all angles unchanged. Areas therefore scale by k squared. Reading any figure means asking what survives once a single uniform change of scale is permitted across the whole plane consistently.

label: The Dilatation
notes: The dilatation, or central similarity, fixes a center O and sends each point P along its own ray to O plus k times the displacement. Every line maps to a parallel line, and lengths scale by the absolute value of k. The sign of k decides whether image points fall on the same or opposite side of O.

label: Two Centers of Similitude
notes: Two unequal non-concentric circles are related by exactly two dilatations. The external center uses a positive ratio pairing radius points in the same direction, while the internal center uses a negative ratio pairing opposite radius points. Both centers lie on the line of centers, and corresponding points stay collinear with them throughout.

label: The Spiral Similarity
notes: A direct similarity that is not a pure dilatation is a spiral similarity: a rotation through angle theta combined with a dilatation of ratio mu about one fixed center. In complex coordinates it reads z maps to a z plus b. Every orbit around the center turns by theta and scales by mu at each step.

label: The Fixed Center
notes: Writing a direct similarity as z prime equals a z plus b, whenever a is not one the equation has a unique solution z0 equals b over one minus a. This is the invariant center about which the whole transformation is a clean dilative rotation. Only the isometric translation edge case, with a equal to one, lacks such a fixed point.

label: Direct versus Opposite
notes: Orientation splits similarities in two. A direct similarity z maps to a z plus b has linear determinant the modulus of a squared, so oriented area keeps its sign. An opposite similarity z maps to a times the conjugate of z plus b has determinant minus that value, reversing every triangle's sense. The determinant sign is the decisive test.

label: The Dilative Reflection
notes: The opposite counterpart of the spiral similarity is the dilative reflection: a dilatation combined with a reflection in a line through the fixed center. It scales by the ratio mu while flipping handedness. Like its direct cousin it possesses a single fixed point unless it degenerates into a pure glide reflection isometry.

label: The Nine-Point Center
notes: The nine-point center N is a center of similitude in disguise. The half-turn dilatation about the centroid with ratio negative one half, and the dilatation about the orthocenter with ratio one half, both land on one circle of radius half the circumradius. Hence N is the midpoint of O and H along the Euler line.

label: Ratios of Length and Area
notes: Because a similarity multiplies every length by k, any ratio of two corresponding lengths equals k and any ratio of two lengths within a single figure is preserved exactly. Areas scale by k squared, so area ratios are likewise invariant. This is why similar triangles share equal angles and proportional sides throughout the plane.

label: Summary and Classification
notes: Every plane similarity is a dilatation, a spiral similarity, or a dilative reflection, together with the isometries as the ratio-one case. Direct maps preserve orientation and, when not isometries, have a unique fixed center; opposite maps reverse it. Length and area ratios survive, anchoring applications from similar triangles to the nine-point center.
